course.description: Text and dates are where "works on my machine" lives. A formatted price that prints `2,50` in Berlin, a parsed date that quietly turns 31 February into 29 February, a due date computed from `LocalDate.now()` that no test can pin down — none of these crash. lessons.title: Strings and Time
lessons.explanation:
# 04 · Strings and Time

Text and dates are where "works on my machine" lives. A formatted price
that prints `2,50` in Berlin, a parsed date that quietly turns 31 February
into 29 February, a due date computed from `LocalDate.now()` that no test
can pin down — none of these crash. They just make the program wrong
somewhere else, later. This module is about making text and time
*deterministic*.

## The mental model

### 1 · Locale is an input — pass it

```java
String.format("%.2f", 2.5);                  // "2,50" on a German machine
String.format(Locale.ROOT, "%.2f", 2.5);     // "2.50" everywhere
"QUIT".toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT);             // never the Turkish dotless ı
DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("EEE", Locale.ENGLISH);
```

Anything machine-readable (files, logs, ids, tests) uses `Locale.ROOT` or
an explicit locale. Only human-facing text uses the user's locale — on
purpose, never by default.

### 2 · Pick the time type that matches the fact

| type | is | use it for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `LocalDate` | a calendar date, no zone | due dates, birthdays, billing days |
| `LocalDateTime` | date + wall-clock time, no zone | rarely right on its own |
| `Instant` | a point on the global timeline | timestamps, logs |
| `ZonedDateTime` | instant + zone rules | "9am in Tokyo" |
| `Period` | years/months/days | "one month later" |
| `Duration` | exact seconds | timeouts, elapsed time |

All of them are **immutable**: `date.plusDays(1)` returns a new date and
leaves `date` alone.

### 3 · "Now" is a dependency

```java
LocalDate.now();          // untestable — the answer changes daily
LocalDate.now(clock);     // production: Clock.systemDefaultZone()
                          // tests: Clock.fixed(Instant.parse(...), zone)
```

### 4 · Parse strictly, format explicitly

```java
var IN = DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("dd/MM/uuuu")
                          .withResolverStyle(ResolverStyle.STRICT);
```

## The details that bite

1. **`split` takes a regex.** `"a|b".split("|")` splits between every
   character. Escape: `split("\\|")`.
2. **`split` drops trailing empty strings** unless you pass a negative
   limit: `split("\\|", -1)`.
3. **`Matcher.find()` is not anchored**; `matches()` is. Validate with
   `matches`, scan with `find` and `\b`.
4. **The default resolver is SMART**: `31/02/2024` parses as
   `2024-02-29`. Use `ResolverStyle.STRICT` for user input.
5. **With STRICT, `yyyy` rejects every date.** `y` is year-of-era; use
   `uuuu`.
6. **`plusMonths` clamps, and chained clamps drift.** Compute each date
   in a schedule from the anchor: `first.plusMonths(i)`.
7. **`-5 / 100` is `0`**, and `0` has no sign: format negatives from the
   absolute value.
8. **`"%-10s"` pads but doesn't cut**; `"%-10.10s"` does both.

## Exercises

| # | file | ★ | what you build |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 01 | `01-receipt-line.java` | ★☆☆ | cents as text, and a receipt line padded with dots |
| 02 | `02-split-and-parse.java` | ★★☆ | a `title|author|year` reader/writer that round-trips |
| 03 | `03-fixed-width-table.java` | ★☆☆ | report rows that look the same in every locale |
| 04 | `04-order-ids.java` | ★★☆ | validate, extract and scan order ids with regex |
| 05 | `05-due-dates.java` | ★☆☆ | due dates, overdue days, weekends with LocalDate |
| 06 | `06-strict-dates.java` | ★★☆ | parse typed dates strictly, label them in English |
| 07 | `07-injected-clock.java` | ★★☆ | late fees against an injected Clock, zones included |
| 08 | `08-billing-schedule.java` | ★★★ | month-end billing that never drifts, and Period text |

Do the warm-ups and core in order. Stretch if time allows.

---

**Next:** `bootcamp/05-classes-records-enums`

unit.title: Late fees, on a clock you control

javabootcamp/04-strings-and-time/01-rece.instructions:
**Concepts:** StringBuilder · String.repeat · cents to text · sign handling  
**Level:** ★☆☆ warm-up

An expense tracker prints receipts. Write formatCents: whole cents as
text with exactly two decimals (never via double). Then write
receiptLine: the item on the left, the price on the right, dots between,
exactly `width` characters long. There is always at least one dot; when
the item is too long, cut it short to make room.

    formatCents(250)                    → "2.50"
    formatCents(-5)                     → "-0.05"
    receiptLine("Milk", 250, 16)        → "Milk........2.50"
    receiptLine("Chocolate", 450, 10)   → "Choco.4.50"

hint: -5 / 100 is 0, and 0 has no sign.
javabootcamp/04-strings-and-time/01-rece.explanation:
Money stays in integer cents until the last moment, and the last moment
is this method: split into whole units (cents / 100) and the remainder
(cents % 100), then zero-pad the remainder to two digits.
The sign is the trap. For -5 cents, -5 / 100 is 0 and -5 % 100 is -5,
so the naive "units + "." + pad(rest)" prints "0.-5" or "0.05" — the
minus sign is lost because 0 cannot carry it. Take the sign first,
then work with the absolute value. Use a long for that absolute value:
Math.abs(Integer.MIN_VALUE) is still negative in int.
String.format(Locale.ROOT, "%d.%02d", ...) does the padding; ROOT keeps
digits ASCII whatever the machine's locale is.
receiptLine is arithmetic on lengths: dots = width - item - price. If
that is under 1, shorten the item to width - price - 1 characters.
"x".repeat(n) (Java 11+) builds the dots; StringBuilder joins the
three parts without creating intermediate strings — for three parts
plain + is just as good, and the compiler emits a StringBuilder anyway.

javabootcamp/04-strings-and-time/02-spli.instructions:
**Concepts:** String.split · regex metacharacters · parseInt · round-trips  
**Level:** ★★☆ core

A library tracker saves books as "title|author|year" lines. Write
parseLine: exactly three fields, each trimmed; a blank title or author,
a year that is not a whole number, or the wrong number of fields throws
IllegalArgumentException (for a bad year, the message mentions "year").
Then write toLine, the inverse — refusing any field that contains "|".
The record Book is defined above the code you edit.

    parseLine("Dune | Frank Herbert | 1965")
        → Book[title=Dune, author=Frank Herbert, year=1965]
    parseLine("Dune|Herbert")         → IllegalArgumentException
    toLine(new Book("Emma", "Austen", 1815)) → "Emma|Austen|1815"

hint: split takes a REGEX, and | means "or" in a regex.
javabootcamp/04-strings-and-time/02-spli.explanation:
String.split's argument is a regular expression, and "|" is the regex
for "empty OR empty" — it matches between every character, so
"a|b".split("|") is [a, |, b]. Escape it: split("\\|"), or quote it
with Pattern.quote("|"). The same goes for ".", "+", "*", "$", "?".
split also silently DROPS trailing empty strings: "Dune|Herbert|"
.split("\\|") has two parts, not three. Passing a negative limit,
split("\\|", -1), keeps them, so a missing year shows up as a blank
field you can report precisely instead of a vague "wrong count".
Integer.parseInt throws NumberFormatException — which IS an
IllegalArgumentException subclass, but its message ("For input string:
...") says nothing about which field was wrong. Catch it and rethrow
with context, passing the original as the cause so the stack trace
keeps the detail.
toLine must refuse a "|" inside a field: writing it would produce a
line that parses back as four fields. Any format you write, you must
be able to read back — the round-trip test pins that down.

javabootcamp/04-strings-and-time/03-fixe.instructions:
**Concepts:** String.format · width and precision · Locale.ROOT · grouping  
**Level:** ★☆☆ warm-up

An order report prints fixed-width rows. Write row: the name left-
aligned in 10 columns (cut at 10), the quantity right-aligned in 4, the
unit price right-aligned in 8 with 2 decimals, separated by "|". Then
write total: cents as an amount with thousands separators. Both must
look the same on every machine, whatever its locale.

    row("Tea", 3, 2.5)          → "Tea       |   3|    2.50"
    row("Earl Grey Tea", 12, 10) → "Earl Grey |  12|   10.00"
    total(123456789)            → "1,234,567.89"

hint: String.format without a Locale uses the machine's default one.
javabootcamp/04-strings-and-time/03-fixe.explanation:
Format specifiers are %[flags][width][.precision]conversion. "%-10s"
left-aligns a string in 10 columns, and adding a precision to a string
conversion TRUNCATES it: "%-10.10s" pads to 10 and cuts at 10. "%4d"
right-aligns an int in 4; "%8.2f" right-aligns a number in 8 with 2
decimals; "%,d" inserts grouping separators.
The locale is the trap. String.format(fmt, ...) uses the default
locale, so on a German machine 2.5 prints as "2,50" and 1234567 groups
as "1.234.567" — your report changes depending on where it runs, and a
test that passed on your laptop fails in CI. Pass Locale.ROOT for
anything machine-readable or test-pinned; pass the user's locale on
purpose when the output is for a human in that locale.
The tests switch the default locale to Germany for a moment (and put
it back in a finally) to prove the output does not move.
total keeps money in integer cents: "%,d.%02d" with cents / 100 and
cents % 100 — no double ever touches it. (Prices here are doubles only
because this exercise is about formatting; module 07 does money
properly.)

javabootcamp/04-strings-and-time/04-orde.instructions:
**Concepts:** regex · Pattern/Matcher · matches vs find · groups · \b  
**Level:** ★★☆ core

An order management tool uses ids like ORD-2024-000123: "ORD", a dash,
a four-digit year, a dash, a six-digit sequence. Write isOrderId (the
WHOLE string must be an id), sequenceOf (the sequence number of a valid
id; anything else → IllegalArgumentException) and findOrderIds (every
id mentioned in free text, in order, ignoring ids glued to other
letters or digits).

    isOrderId("ORD-2024-000123")     → true
    isOrderId(" ORD-2024-000123")    → false
    sequenceOf("ORD-2024-000123")    → 123
    findOrderIds("re ORD-2024-000001, ORD-2023-999999.")
        → [ORD-2024-000001, ORD-2023-999999]

hint: Matcher.matches() is anchored at both ends; find() is not.
javabootcamp/04-strings-and-time/04-orde.explanation:
Compile a regex once into a static final Pattern; Pattern.compile is
the expensive part, and String.matches(regex) recompiles every call.
Matcher.matches() must match the ENTIRE input, so no ^ and $ are
needed there. find() looks for the next match ANYWHERE, which is what
you want for scanning text and exactly wrong for validating: a
validator built on find() accepts "xxORD-2024-000123xx".
For scanning, the boundaries move into the pattern: \b is a word
boundary (between a word char and a non-word char), so
\bORD-\d{4}-\d{6}\b refuses "XORD-..." and a seven-digit sequence —
both would otherwise yield a match hiding inside a longer token.
Groups pull pieces out: in ORD-(\d{4})-(\d{6}), group(2) is the
sequence. Integer.parseInt("000123") is 123; leading zeros are fine.
In a Java string literal every regex backslash is doubled: "\\d{4}".
(Java 15 text blocks don't change that.) And a classic false friend:
"." in a regex is ANY character — a literal dot is "\\.".

javabootcamp/04-strings-and-time/05-due-.instructions:
**Concepts:** LocalDate · plusDays · ChronoUnit.DAYS.between · DayOfWeek  
**Level:** ★☆☆ warm-up

A library tracker lends books for a number of days. Write dueDate
(borrowed plus the loan period), daysOverdue (how many days after the
due date the book came back; on time or early → 0) and isWeekend.

    dueDate(2024-01-25, 14)             → 2024-02-08
    dueDate(2024-02-20, 14)             → 2024-03-05   (leap year!)
    daysOverdue(2024-03-01, 2024-03-04) → 3
    daysOverdue(2024-03-01, 2024-02-27) → 0
    isWeekend(2024-03-02)               → true   (a Saturday)

hint: LocalDate does the calendar for you; never add days by hand.
javabootcamp/04-strings-and-time/05-due-.explanation:
LocalDate is a date with no time and no time zone — exactly what a due
date is. It is immutable: plusDays returns a NEW date, and
`borrowed.plusDays(14);` on its own line does nothing at all (a common
first bug; the result has to be returned or assigned).
plusDays knows month lengths and leap years, so January 25 + 14 lands
in February and 2024-02-20 + 14 counts February 29.
ChronoUnit.DAYS.between(start, end) counts whole days and is negative
when end is before start — clamp with Math.max(0, ...) because "early"
is not "minus three days overdue". (due.until(returned, DAYS) is the
same thing spelled from the other side.)
isWeekend compares DayOfWeek enum constants. Never compare
getDayOfWeek().getValue() with magic numbers or, worse, a day name
string — the name depends on the locale, the enum does not.
Note what is missing: no LocalDate.now(). These methods take the dates
they need as parameters, which is what makes them testable (exercise
07 injects a Clock for the cases that really need "today").

javabootcamp/04-strings-and-time/06-stri.instructions:
**Concepts:** DateTimeFormatter · ResolverStyle.STRICT · uuuu vs yyyy · Locale  
**Level:** ★★☆ core

An expense tracker accepts dates typed as day/month/year. Write
parseDate: exactly "dd/MM/uuuu", and an impossible date like 31/02 is
an error, never quietly "corrected" (DateTimeParseException either way).
Then write label: a date as "Mon 05 Feb 2024", in English on every
machine.

    parseDate("05/02/2024")    → 2024-02-05
    parseDate("31/02/2024")    → DateTimeParseException
    parseDate("2024-02-05")    → DateTimeParseException
    label(2024-02-05)          → "Mon 05 Feb 2024"

hint: the default resolver turns 31 February into 29 February.
javabootcamp/04-strings-and-time/06-stri.explanation:
DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("dd/MM/uuuu") alone parses "31/02/2024"
without complaint and returns 2024-02-29: the default resolver style is
SMART, which clamps an out-of-range day to the end of the month. For
user input that is a silent data change. withResolverStyle(
ResolverStyle.STRICT) makes it an error.
STRICT has a famous sting: with "yyyy" it fails on EVERY date. In
java.time "y" is year-of-ERA, which needs an era (AD/BC) to resolve
strictly, and the pattern has none. "u" is the proleptic year, which
needs nothing else. Use uuuu with STRICT; yyyy with STRICT is a
formatter that rejects everything.
Build the formatters once, as static finals: they are immutable and
thread-safe (unlike the old SimpleDateFormat, which was neither).
For label, EEE and MMM are day and month NAMES, which come from a
locale. ofPattern without one uses the default locale, so a French
machine prints "lun. 05 févr. 2024". Pin it with
ofPattern(pattern, Locale.ENGLISH) whenever the text is part of a file
format, a log line, or a test.

javabootcamp/04-strings-and-time/07-inje.instructions:
**Concepts:** Clock · LocalDate.now(clock) · time zones · testability  
**Level:** ★★☆ core

A library tracker charges late fees as of TODAY. Finish the nested
class LateFees: it is built from a Clock, a fee per day in cents and a
cap. isOverdue(due) is true once today is after the due date; feeFor
(due) is days late times the daily fee, never more than the cap, and 0
when not overdue. "Today" is the clock's date in the clock's zone.

    clock at 2024-03-10 (UTC), 25 cents a day, cap 500
    feeFor(2024-03-07)   → 75
    feeFor(2024-01-01)   → 500
    feeFor(2024-03-10)   → 0

hint: LocalDate.now() reads the real clock; there is an overload.
javabootcamp/04-strings-and-time/07-inje.explanation:
Code that calls LocalDate.now() cannot be tested: the answer changes
every day, and you cannot make "today" be a leap day or a year end on
demand. java.time's answer is Clock — an object that answers "what
instant is it, and in which zone?" Every now() has a now(Clock)
overload. Production passes Clock.systemDefaultZone(); tests pass
Clock.fixed(instant, zone) and get the same answer forever.
The class takes the Clock in its constructor and keeps it in a final
field: dependency injection without a framework.
The zone matters, and the last test proves it. The instant
2024-03-10T23:30Z is still March 10 in London but already March 11 in
Tokyo. LocalDate.now(clock) uses the clock's zone, so a Tokyo clock
makes a book due March 10 one day late. That is the right answer for a
library in Tokyo, and the reason "today" is never a bare instant.
Fee arithmetic: days late from ChronoUnit.DAYS.between(due, today);
long times int is long; Math.min against the cap; Math.toIntExact to
come back to int loudly rather than by truncation.

javabootcamp/04-strings-and-time/08-bill.instructions:
**Concepts:** plusMonths · month-end clamping · drift · Period  
**Level:** ★★★ stretch

A bank simulator bills monthly on the day the account opened. Write
billingDates: the first `count` billing dates starting at `first`. A
short month bills on its last day, but the next month goes back to the
original day — the schedule never drifts. Then write describeGap: the
calendar distance between two dates as years, months and days, leaving
out zero parts, singular or plural; no difference at all → "0 days".

    billingDates(2024-01-31, 4)
        → [2024-01-31, 2024-02-29, 2024-03-31, 2024-04-30]
    describeGap(2024-01-31, 2024-03-01)   → "1 month 1 day"
    describeGap(2023-01-15, 2025-01-18)   → "2 years 3 days"

hint: compute each date from `first`, not from the previous date.
javabootcamp/04-strings-and-time/08-bill.explanation:
plusMonths clamps: January 31 plus one month is February 29 (in 2024),
because there is no February 31. That is the right answer for ONE step.
The trap is chaining: date = date.plusMonths(1) in a loop gives Jan 31,
Feb 29, Mar 29, Apr 29... — once clamped, the schedule has forgotten
its anchor day and drifts for the rest of its life. Computing every
date from the anchor, first.plusMonths(i), clamps each month
independently and lands back on the 31st whenever the month has one.
The general lesson: in a recurrence, derive each step from the origin,
not from the last (possibly rounded) step. Money schedules, retries and
animation timers all have the same bug.
Period is the calendar-based amount of time — years, months, days —
as opposed to Duration, which is exact seconds. Period.between(a, b)
counts whole months first, then the leftover days, so Jan 31 to Mar 1
is 1 month and 1 day. (It does NOT normalise "14 months" into a year:
between gives you already-normalised parts, but Period.ofMonths(14)
stays 14 months until you call normalized().)
describeGap is then small string assembly: a part per non-zero field,
pluralised, joined with spaces, with "0 days" for the empty case.
